chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: George Treadwell offers him Sarah Vaughan's piano chair, with Jimmy Jones ill
summary: Treadwell says Jones will die of lung cancer, but Jones recovers; Malachi stays with Sarah almost two years.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: But the last I worked with him, we played a job in Birdland. While we were in Birdland... It was just before the turn of the year from '51 to '52. George Treadwell, who was Sarah Vaughan's husband, called me and asked me if I would come with Sarah as her accompanist. Jimmy Jones, the pianist that had been with her, was very ill and was in the hospital for an operation, and the situation was such as they thought that he would be there for quite some time. So I told him I would think about it.

Then I asked him, 'Well, just how long do you think?' -- because he said quite some time, and I thought he meant about two or three weeks, or something like that. So he made a statement, and one that I think nobody should ever make. He said, 'Jimmy Jones is not coming back at all.' I said, 'Why?' He said Jimmy had lung cancer, and they were going to take out a lung or something like that, and he says, 'To tell you the truth, Jimmy Jones is going to die, and if you want the job, it's yours.'
Well, Jimmy Jones was a friend of mine, and had been a

friend of mine since back during the Chicago days... Which, if I didn't mention it, when I was in Chicago with Trummy Young, one of the groups there was Stuff Smith, who had a trio with Jimmy Jones and John Levy playing bass -- Jimmy Jones playing piano and Stuff Smith, violin. So I had known Jimmy for quite a while, and we were good friends, and we had just a real piano comrade thing going. So this was a dreadful thing to hear. But in hearing it, there was nothing that... You know, you can't do anything about things like that.

So I took the job. And I stayed with Sarah for the better part of two years. Jimmy Jones endured this operation and everything, and he came out of the hospital, and he was well, and he came back to his job. If I can get ahead a little bit, to just complete this story, this is in 1954. I think five or six years later, during 1960, George Treadwell died of cancer, and Jimmy Jones lived a good 20 or 25 years after that. So I would say to anybody, don't ever predict anybody's death, because no one knows when that's going to happen.
